title: Generating types from OpenAPI; a typed API client
summary: An OpenAPI document is the contract between server and client. openapi-typescript turns it into types with no run-time code, and a small generic client checks paths, parameters and per-status bodies at compile time. Nothing checks the server at run time, so drift needs a validator or a test.

examples.title: A generic client over generated paths: wrong paths and params don't compile

annotations.note: The shape openapi-typescript emits, abbreviated: paths keyed by the literal path template, then the method, then parameters and responses keyed by status code, each with content keyed by media type. The unabridged generated file works with the same client unchanged.
The client is pure indexing into the generated types. Reply maps every documented status S to { status: S; body } and takes the union of them, a discriminated union on status built from the contract.
P is inferred from the path literal, so path is checked against the contract and params gets that path's parameter type. Only the fetch function is injected, as in the earlier lessons.

Types are erased, so the client can't know at run time which statuses the spec lists, and this cast is unavoidable. A status the spec doesn't mention, such as a proxy's 502, is cast all the same. Check the status first, or validate (example 2).
Before the status check, body is Order | Problem; after reply.status === 200 it is Order. The error path is as typed as the happy path.
Mistakes that a hand-written fetch(`/order/${id}`) would send to the server fail the build instead. Renaming a path in the spec and regenerating turns every stale call site into a compile error.

examples.title: When the server drifts from the spec: nil slices and int64 ids

annotations.note: This is the generator's output for type: integer, format: int64. JSON numbers are doubles in JavaScript, so the format survives only as a comment.
Two classic Go-side deviations. encoding/json writes a nil slice as null, and an int64 as a number, however large. Both are legal JSON, and neither matches the spec.
The cast succeeds, as every generated client's does. The id is silently rounded to the nearest double, and items.length throws a TypeError far from the response that caused it.

Annotating the schema with the generated type ties the two definitions: if the spec changes and the schema no longer produces an Order, tsc rejects it. At run time the schema reports both problems with their paths. int() accepts only safe integers, so the rounded id fails instead of passing as the wrong number.

Fix the contract, not the client. Go initializes the slice (Items: []string{}), and large ids travel as strings (the ,string tag option, type: string in the spec). BigInt does exact arithmetic when you need it.

use_cases: A frontend and a Go backend developed in parallel: the spec in the repo is what both sides compile against
Calling a third-party API that publishes an OpenAPI document, without writing its types by hand
Typed error handling: per-status response types for 404, 409 and 422 problem bodies
CI checks: regenerate types and fail on a diff when the spec changed but the client didn't
strengths: One spec drives server stubs, client types, documentation and mock servers, instead of each side retyping the shapes
Renamed fields and removed endpoints become compile errors after regenerating, not production bugs
openapi-typescript emits types only, so the client costs no bundle size beyond your fetch wrapper
Per-status response types make the error paths as typed as the happy path
weaknesses: Generated types check nothing at run time: a server that deviates from its own spec goes unnoticed without validation
A spec written by hand next to the code drifts like any other copy: generate one side from the other, or test against it
JSON semantics leak through: int64 ids, nullable vs optional, Go's nil slices and omitempty
The generated types are deeply nested, and helpers that index into them are hard to read without a library such as openapi-fetch

pitfalls.title: Treating generated types as validation
pitfalls.detail: The types describe what the spec promises. If the server's real behaviour matters, validate responses at the client edge, at least in development and tests.

pitfalls.title: int64 ids as JSON numbers
pitfalls.detail: Above 2^53 - 1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), JSON.parse rounds silently. Send such ids as strings.
pitfalls.bad: ID int64 `json:"id"`   // spec: type: integer, format: int64

pitfalls.title: Go nil slices and omitempty
pitfalls.detail: A nil slice marshals as null, and omitempty drops false, 0, "" and empty slices entirely, so a field the spec marks required can be null or missing. Initialize slices, and use omitempty only on optional fields.

pitfalls.title: Editing the generated file
pitfalls.detail: The next regeneration erases the edit. Change the spec, or wrap the generated types in your own module.

quiz.q: The client uses types generated by openapi-typescript. What checks at run time that a response matches components["schemas"]["Order"]?
options: The generated code validates each response
Nothing, unless you add a validator
quiz.why: openapi-typescript emits types only, and types are erased. The run-time check has to be code, such as a zod schema.

quiz.q: A Go handler returns ID int64 = 9007199254740993 as a JSON number. What does JSON.parse produce?
quiz.why: JSON numbers become doubles, and above 2^53 - 1 not every integer is representable: the value rounds to the nearest double, silently.

quiz.q: A Go struct has Items []string `json:"items"` and the handler never sets it. What does the client receive?
quiz.why: encoding/json writes a nil slice as null. The key would be missing only with omitempty, and [] needs an initialized empty slice.

quiz.q: In example 1, why does reply.body.customer fail to compile before checking reply.status?
options: body is unknown until it is validated
body is the union Order | Problem until the status narrows it
customer is optional in the spec
quiz.why: Reply has one member per documented status. Comparing status with 200 selects the member whose body is Order.
